Electric Dress, a wearable sculpture of painted light bulbs and tubes that she wore at the second Gutai exhibition in 1956, linked the body, technology and painting. In later decades she painted networks of coloured circles and lines derived from its wiring. Her works are still under copyright.

name: Yayoi Kusama
bio: Japanese artist of polka dots, mirrored infinity rooms and Infinity Net paintings, a figure of the New York avant-garde of the 1960s.
bio_full: Kusama was born in Matsumoto to a family of seed merchants. She has described hallucinations from childhood of patterns covering everything around her. After studying nihonga in Kyoto she moved to New York in 1958, where she painted vast Infinity Nets, made soft sculptures covered with phalluses, staged naked happenings and created the first mirrored infinity environments. She returned to Japan in 1973 and since 1977 has lived by choice in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo, working in a studio nearby.

Kusama's art of repetition and accumulation, which she links to self-obliteration, anticipated Minimalism, Pop and installation art. Long overlooked, she was rediscovered from the late 1980s and represented Japan at the Venice Biennale in 1993, becoming one of the most popular living artists. Her works are under copyright.

name: An Gyeon
bio: Court painter of early Joseon, painter of the Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land (1447), the foundation of Korean landscape painting.
bio_full: An Gyeon served in the Dohwaseo, the Joseon royal bureau of painting, under King Sejong and his successors and rose to an unusually high rank for a painter. He was a protégé of Prince Anpyeong, Sejong's third son, a great calligrapher and collector who owned Chinese paintings by Guo Xi and others. Few facts about his life are documented.

In 1447 Prince Anpyeong described a dream of wandering into the peach blossom paradise of Tao Yuanming's fable, and An Gyeon painted it in three days. The handscroll, with inscriptions by the prince and twenty-one scholars, shows how An Gyeon adapted Guo Xi's style into a distinctly Korean idiom. It left Korea, probably during the Japanese invasions, and is now in Tenri University Library in Japan. His manner, the An Gyeon school, dominated early Joseon landscape.

name: Jeong Seon
bio: Painter who created true-view landscape painting (jingyeong sansu), depicting the real mountains of Korea rather than idealised Chinese scenery.
bio_full: Jeong Seon, known by his pen name Gyeomjae, was born to an impoverished yangban family in Seoul and grew up near Mount Inwang. He studied Neo-Confucianism with the circle of Kim Chang-hyeop, whose members promoted a culture rooted in Korea. Through their recommendation he entered government service and held local posts, painting all his life. He travelled several times to the Diamond Mountains (Geumgangsan), which became his great subject.

Jeong Seon painted real Korean places with a mixture of Chinese Southern school techniques and inventions of his own, such as the vertical, crystalline strokes for granite peaks and wet dotting for forested hills. His Inwangsan after Rain (1751) and Complete View of the Diamond Mountains (1734) are National Treasures. He made Korean landscape a subject in its own right and inspired a generation of true-view painters.

name: Kim Hong-do
bio: Joseon court painter, master of genre scenes of ordinary Korean life as well as landscapes and Daoist immortals.
bio_full: Kim Hong-do, known as Danwon, studied as a youth with the scholar-painter Kang Se-hwang and entered the royal painting bureau. He painted royal portraits for King Yeongjo and King Jeongjo, who greatly favoured him, and in 1789 was sent with an embassy to Japan to make maps of Tsushima. He served briefly as a county magistrate. His later life was difficult, and the date of his death is uncertain.

Kim Hong-do's album of genre paintings in the National Museum of Korea shows wrestlers, dancers, blacksmiths, a village school and farmers at work in quick, humorous sketches without background, full of observation of gesture. He was equally skilled in landscape and figure painting, and he is regarded with Jeong Seon and Shin Yun-bok as one of the three great masters of late Joseon painting.

name: Shin Yun-bok
bio: Late Joseon painter known as Hyewon, famous for elegant, colourful scenes of romance, courtesans and the leisure of the aristocracy.
bio_full: Shin Yun-bok was the son of the court painter Shin Han-pyeong. Almost nothing about his life is documented; according to a common but unverified story he was expelled from the royal painting bureau for painting improper subjects. His dates are uncertain.

Unlike Kim Hong-do's rustic scenes, Shin Yun-bok painted the urban world of yangban men and gisaeng entertainers: picnics, moonlit meetings, the Dano festival with women bathing and swinging, with fine line, bright colour and detailed settings. His album in the Kansong Art Museum is a National Treasure, and his Portrait of a Beauty is one of the best-known Korean paintings.

name: Kim Jeong-hui
bio: Scholar, epigrapher, calligrapher and painter (pen name Chusa) who created the Chusa calligraphic style and painted the literati masterpiece Sehando.
bio_full: Kim Jeong-hui came from an aristocratic family related to the royal house. In 1809 he accompanied his father on an embassy to Beijing, where he met the Qing scholars Weng Fanggang and Ruan Yuan and became an enthusiast for the study of ancient inscriptions; back in Korea he identified the Bukhansan monument of King Jinheung of Silla. He held high office but fell victim to factional politics and spent nine years in exile on Jeju Island (1840–48) and later more in the north.

Kim Jeong-hui developed the Chusa style of calligraphy, based on ancient clerical script, with angular, unbalanced, powerful strokes. As a painter he advocated the Chinese literati ideal of expressing the mind, and his ink orchids and Sehando are its purest Korean expression. He was the central figure of Korean scholarly culture in the nineteenth century.

name: Yun Du-seo
bio: Joseon scholar-painter, great-grandson of the poet Yun Seon-do, whose unflinching self-portrait is one of the masterpieces of Korean portraiture.
bio_full: Yun Du-seo was born into the eminent Haenam Yun family and passed the lower civil examination in 1693, but because his faction, the Southerners, was out of power he never held office. He lived in Seoul and later on the family estate in Haenam, studying geography, astronomy, mathematics and painting in the spirit of practical learning (silhak). His son Yun Deok-hui and grandson Yun Yong were also painters.

Yun Du-seo painted horses, figures and early genre scenes of ordinary people working, which anticipated the genre painting of Kim Hong-do. His Self-portrait, owned by his descendants in Haenam and designated a National Treasure, shows only his face and beard, staring at the viewer with extraordinary intensity, painted in fine lines.

name: Park Soo-keun
bio: Self-taught Korean painter of ordinary people, women and children, painted in a thick granite-like texture that recalls ancient stone carvings.
bio_full: Park Soo-keun grew up in poverty in Gangwon province and was largely self-taught; he decided to become a painter after seeing a reproduction of Millet's Angelus. He exhibited at the Joseon Art Exhibition from 1932. After the Korean War, during which he fled south, he lived in Seoul working for the US Army post exchange painting portraits, and sold paintings mainly to foreigners. He died poor in 1965.

Park's paintings show women carrying babies or selling vegetables, children and bare trees in muted earth tones with a heavily layered, rough surface inspired by Silla stone reliefs. They capture the hardship and dignity of postwar Korean life, and he is now regarded as one of the most beloved Korean painters. His works are under copyright.

name: Lee Ufan
bio: Korean painter, sculptor and philosopher, a leading theorist of Japan's Mono-ha movement, known for the From Point and From Line series.
bio_full: Lee Ufan studied painting briefly in Seoul and moved to Japan in 1956, where he studied philosophy at Nihon University. In the late 1960s he became the principal theorist of Mono-ha (School of Things), writing essays on encounter and relation, and making works of stones, steel plates and glass. He has taught at Tama Art University and lived between Japan, Korea and Paris. A museum devoted to him on Naoshima opened in 2010.

Lee's paintings of the 1970s, From Point and From Line, consist of marks repeated as the brush runs out of pigment, recording time and the act of painting; his later Correspondence and Dialogue works reduce this to a few strokes. He was also associated with Korean Dansaekhwa. His works are under copyright.

name: Nam June Paik
bio: Korean-born artist regarded as the founder of video art, a member of Fluxus, whose works include TV Buddha and vast multi-monitor installations.
bio_full: Nam June Paik was born in Seoul to a wealthy family that fled the Korean War to Hong Kong and Japan. He studied aesthetics at the University of Tokyo and music in Germany, where he met John Cage and joined the Fluxus movement. In 1963 he showed altered television sets in Wuppertal, and after moving to New York in 1964 he used one of the first portable video cameras, working with the cellist Charlotte Moorman and engineers on video synthesisers. He died in Miami in 2006.

Paik foresaw the importance of television and electronic networks, coining the phrase electronic superhighway. TV Buddha (1974), in which a statue of the Buddha watches its own image on a monitor, is a meditation on technology and contemplation. His works are under copyright.
